content: In endemic areas, mass immunization of children and pigs with the Japanese Encephalitis (JE) vaccine is recommended, as well as vaccination for travelers visiting these regions. The Nipah virus (NiV) derives its name from Sungai Nipah, a village in Malaysia where pig farmers first fell ill with encephalitis. Since then, outbreaks of NiV have occurred almost annually in South Asia, causing severe disease and death, making it a significant emerging public health concern. The virus infects a wide range of animals, including pigs, and has led to substantial economic losses for pig farmers in Malaysia. Countries affected by NiV in the Asia-Pacific region include Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, and Singapore. The virus belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family, with fruit bats of the genus Pteropus (flying foxes) serving as the primary reservoir. NiV can infect pigs, dogs, cats, horses, and humans through the consumption of food or drink contaminated with bat secretions such as saliva or urine. In Bangladesh, the cultural practice of drinking raw date palm sap is a major risk factor for human infection. Human-to-human transmission of NiV has been reported in recent outbreaks, posing a risk to healthcare workers who may acquire the virus through contact with infected secretions, excretions, blood, or tissues. Infected bats shed the virus in their saliva, urine, semen, and excreta but remain asymptomatic carriers. NiV is transmitted to humans either from animals (via contact with urine, saliva, or contaminated materials) or from other humans. In Bangladesh, approximately half of the reported cases between 2001 and 2008 were attributed to human-to-human transmission. The incubation period for NiV infection ranges from 4 to 21 days. Symptoms in humans vary from asymptomatic infection to fatal encephalitis. Initially, infected individuals develop flu-like symptoms such as fever, headache, muscle pain, vomiting, and sore throat. This may progress to dizziness, drowsiness, altered consciousness, and neurological signs indicative of acute encephalitis. Severe cases may involve atypical pneumonia, acute respiratory distress, seizures, and coma within 24–48 hours. Approximately 40–75% of symptomatic cases result in death. There is no specific treatment or vaccine for NiV; management involves intensive supportive care and symptom treatment. Healthcare workers should adhere to standard precautions when caring for patients with suspected or confirmed NiV infection and when handling specimens. Protective equipment, such as gloves and masks, should be used when caring for ill individuals, and hand hygiene should be practiced after visiting sick patients. Coronaviruses are a group of viruses that infect humans and animals, typically causing mild to moderate respiratory tract infections, though they can also cause gastroenteritis. Human coronaviruses were first identified in the 1960s and are responsible for a significant proportion of common colds in adults. Novel human coronaviruses have emerged in recent years, jumping from animals to humans and causing serious socioeconomic consequences. Notable examples include Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (SARS-CoV) and Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV). SARS-CoV first appeared in November 2002 in Guangdong Province, China, and subsequently spread to 26 countries, resulting in over 8,000 cases in 2003. The virus is believed to have originated in bats, with civet cats acting as intermediate hosts. SARS is a rare disease, with reappearances linked to laboratory accidents or animal-to-human transmission. The elderly and immunosuppressed individuals are particularly vulnerable. Transmission occurs through inhalation of respiratory droplets from infected individuals, though other modes of transmission remain unclear. The incubation period is 2–14 days, and symptoms include fever, muscle pain, lethargy, cough, and sore throat, which may progress to severe respiratory disease and pneumonia. There is no specific treatment for SARS; supportive therapy is required. MERS-CoV, first identified in 2012, has caused 177 laboratory-confirmed cases and 74 deaths globally as of December 2013. Human cases have been reported in 11 countries, primarily in the Middle East, with links to camels as a likely source of infection. The virus is thought to be of animal origin, but the exact mode of transmission remains unclear. Individuals with diabetes, chronic lung disease, renal failure, or weakened immune systems are at higher risk of severe disease. The incubation period is 2–10 days, and symptoms include fever, cough, and breathing difficulties, often progressing to pneumonia. Severe complications include kidney failure and acute respiratory distress. There is no specific treatment for MERS-CoV; supportive care is the mainstay of management. Rabies is a preventable viral zoonotic disease that is almost always fatal once clinical symptoms develop. It causes approximately 55,000 deaths globally each year, with children being the primary victims. The virus is transmitted through bites or scratches from infected animals, primarily dogs. The incubation period is typically 4–8 weeks but can extend to several years. Symptoms include pain or tingling at the bite site, hydrophobia (fear of water), restlessness, excessive salivation, convulsions, and death. Immediate post-bite treatment, including vaccination and rabies immunoglobulin, is highly effective in preventing the disease. However, there is no cure once symptoms develop. Rift Valley Fever (RVF) is a viral disease that primarily affects livestock but can also infect humans. Outbreaks are often preceded by heavy rains and manifest as mass mortality among young animals or waves of unexplained abortions in livestock. Human infection occurs through contact with infected animals or mosquito bites. Most human cases are mild, presenting with flu-like symptoms, but severe cases can involve ocular, meningoencephalitis, or hemorrhagic syndromes. There is no specific treatment or vaccine for human use; supportive care is the mainstay of management. Viral hepatitis is an infectious disease causing liver inflammation, often presenting with jaundice, loss of appetite, nausea, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort. There are five types of hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, D, and E), each with distinct transmission routes. Hepatitis A and E are foodborne and waterborne, causing acute illness, while hepatitis B, C, and D are transmitted through blood, contaminated medical equipment, sexual contact, or mother-to-child transmission. Chronic hepatitis B and C infections can lead to liver damage, cirrhosis, and liver cancer.
